articles.title: Kart que mistura realidade e videogame vira negócio itinerante e fatura R$ 120 mil por mês | G1
articles.standfirst: Empreendedor investiu R$ 1 milhão em parque de realidade virtual e adotou modelo itinerante após perceber queda de público em operações fixas. Atrações hoje circulam por shoppings de diferentes cidades.
articles.summary: Empreendedor trouxe tecnologia da China, investiu R$ 1 milhão e criou rede de parques virtuais que percorre cidades brasileiras em busca de novos públicos.
articles.body:
Uma corrida de kart em que os pilotos cruzam cenários pré-históricos, desviam de dinossauros e utilizam poderes dignos de videogame pode parecer ficção.

Mas a experiência já é realidade no Brasil graças à tecnologia de realidade mista, que combina elementos físicos e virtuais em um mesmo ambiente.

Foi nessa tendência que o empreendedor Rodrigo Martins encontrou uma oportunidade de negócio que hoje rende faturamento mensal de R$ 120 mil.

O empresário é dono de um parque de realidade virtual itinerante que leva atrações para diferentes shopping centers do país .

O principal destaque é um kart que mistura pilotagem real com cenários digitais vistos por meio de óculos especiais. A tecnologia é exclusiva da empresa no Brasil , segundo o empreendedor.

A trajetória começou em 2023, quando Rodrigo Martins inaugurou seu primeiro parque de realidade virtual. O sucesso inicial levou o empresário a viajar para a China em busca de novas experiências.

Durante uma das visitas aos fornecedores, surgiu a oportunidade de negociar exclusividade para explorar parte da tecnologia no mercado brasileiro.

Kart em realidade mista vira negócio itinerante e fatura R$ 120 mil por mês — Foto: Reprodução/PEGN

A proposta veio acompanhada de um desafio. Para garantir a exclusividade, o fabricante chinês exigiu uma expansão acelerada da operação . Mesmo ainda no início da jornada, o empreendedor decidiu apostar no crescimento.

“Eu queria uma exclusividade. Então, para eu replicar isso no Brasil todo, ele foi claro: compra mais dez parques. Naquela ânsia de empreendedor eu fui e falei: cinco eu garanto”, conta.

Mais tarde, uma nova visita à China apresentou ao empresário a tecnologia de realidade mista utilizada no kart virtual . A novidade chamou a atenção por conseguir integrar o mundo físico e o digital de forma sincronizada, criando uma experiência imersiva para os participantes.

Segundo Rodrigo Martins, a exclusividade funciona como uma importante barreira competitiva . “A gente fala que está sempre pelo menos um ano na frente da concorrência”, afirma.

Para colocar o projeto em prática, foram investidos cerca de R$ 1 milhão . Os primeiros parques funcionavam de forma fixa em shopping centers do interior paulista. No começo, a novidade atraía grande quantidade de visitantes.

Com o passar do tempo, porém, o fluxo diminuía à medida que o público local já conhecia a atração. Foi dessa constatação que nasceu o modelo itinerante.

“Você começa bem porque é novidade. A cidade está falando do seu negócio. Depois de seis meses, um ano, começa a dar uma caída. Foi aí que veio a ideia de fazer um parque itinerante”, explica.

Desde o ano passado, a operação passou a circular entre diferentes cidades. Para viabilizar a logística, o empreendedor firmou uma sociedade com o dono de uma empresa especializada em eventos .

A estratégia tem permitido renovar constantemente o interesse do público e ampliar a presença da marca em novas regiões.

O modelo também mudou a relação com os shopping centers. Em vez de atuar apenas como locatário, o parque passou a ser visto como um atrativo para aumentar a circulação de consumidores.

“Hoje eu praticamente não pago aluguel. Eles chamam a gente para trazer público para o shopping”, afirma.

Além das pistas de kart em realidade mista, os parques oferecem outras experiências imersivas, como simuladores de montanha-russa e atrações voltadas para diferentes faixas etárias. O ticket médio do kart é de R$ 79,90.

A sazonalidade também faz parte da gestão do negócio . Férias escolares, Dia das Crianças, Black Friday e Natal estão entre os períodos de maior movimento. Já nos meses de menor demanda, a empresa aposta em descontos e promoções durante a semana para atrair visitantes.

Mesmo com a expansão, o empreendedor acredita que o potencial de crescimento ainda está longe do limite. “A gente não rodou nem 1% do que tem para rodar ainda”, diz.

Enquanto leva seus simuladores de cidade em cidade, Rodrigo Martins já prepara o próximo passo. A empresa está desenvolvendo uma nova atração com tecnologia produzida no Brasil, prevista para ser lançada nos próximos meses.

Os detalhes continuam em segredo, mas a estratégia segue a mesma que impulsionou o negócio até aqui: oferecer experiências inéditas para manter o público em movimento e a concorrência sempre alguns passos atrás.

📍 Endereço: Rod. Pres. Dutra, 225, Vila Itapegica (Corredor do Mercado Extra), Guarulhos/SP – CEP: 07034-911

articles.title: Novo lar de Sandro: conheça o 1º Santuário de Elefantes do Brasil, em  | G1
articles.standfirst: Localizado em Chapada dos Guimarães (MT), projeto sem fins lucrativos já resgatou 13 animais e oferece cuidados especializados sem visitação pública.
articles.summary: Localizado em Chapada dos Guimarães (MT), projeto sem fins lucrativos já resgatou 13 animais e oferece cuidados especializados sem visitação pública.
articles.body:
Santuário de Elefantes, em Chapada dos Guimarães — Foto: Santuário de Elefantes/Divulgação

Criado para oferecer uma alternativa ao confinamento, o Santuário de Elefantes Brasil (SEB) atualmente abriga seis elefantas fêmeas e se prepara pra receber o primeiro macho, Sandro , nesta sexta- feira (18). O local não é aberto à visitação pública do turismo tradicional, para que não haja exposição dos animais ao estresse do público ou a rotinas de apresentações.

Localizado em Chapada dos Guimarães , a organização sem fins lucrativos atua na recuperação e no acolhimento de elefantes resgatados, oferecendo um ambiente com vasta vegetação, lagos e estímulos naturais para que os animais recuperem comportamentos típicos da espécie.

Segundo o presidente do SEB, Raphael Bontempi , a proposta do local é garantir proporções e condições de vida que estruturas urbanas de exposição não conseguem alcançar.

"A gente é uma associação, uma ONG sem fins lucrativos. O nosso objetivo é o resgate desses elefantes. A gente nasceu para poder trabalhar com os elefantes da América do Sul, que tínhamos aproximadamente 50 quando começamos o projeto. Agora tem muito menos. A gente resgatou ao redor de 13, que vieram morar aqui no santuário", explica Raphael.

Segundo Raphael, a diferença entre o ambiente do santuário e os recintos tradicionais de cativeiro é um dos pilares para a reabilitação física e psicológica dos elefantes. As áreas destinadas a cada morador contam com dezenas de hectares, permitindo caminhadas longas, exploração de terreno acidentado e contato com diferentes tipos de solo.

Para exemplificar a escala da propriedade, o presidente da instituição compara a área destinada ao mais novo morador do local, o elefante Sandro, que viveu quatro décadas no Parque Zoológico Municipal Quinzinho de Barros e foi transferido nesta quarta-feira (16) para o santuário, com o espaço onde o animal viveu durante anos em São Paulo.

Diferente de zoológicos, o Santuário de Elefantes Brasil não é aberto à visitação pública do turismo tradicional, garantindo que os animais não sejam expostos ao estresse do público ou a rotinas de apresentações.

A dinâmica do espaço é pautada por diretrizes técnicas rigorosas de manejo e proteção:

Estímulo à autonomia: Os animais têm liberdade para decidir quando e onde querem caminhar, banhar-se nos lagos ou descansar, desenvolvendo rotinas próprias.

Redução do estresse do cativeiro: A oferta contínua de estímulos visuais, olfativos e de espaço reduz comportamentos repetitivos (estereotipias) causados pelo tédio e pelo confinamento prolongado.

Equipe multiprofissional: O acompanhamento é feito diariamente por veterinários, biólogos e tratadores especializados na reabilitação de grandes mamíferos.

Segurança e regras de manejo: Os recintos mantêm separações técnicas por espécie e gênero, respeitando a organização social natural dos animais e cumprindo as normas ambientais de licenciamento, que proíbem a reprodução de espécies exóticas em cativeiro.

Apesar disso, o santuário foi alvo de ataques por moradores de Sorocaba no último domingo (14). Dois dias antes da transferência de Sandro ao Santuário, famílias com crianças foram ao zoológico onde ele morava para protestar contra a transferência do elefante Sandro. Os manifestantes levaram cartazes com frases como “Fica, Sandro”, “A vida do Sandro é valiosa para nós” e “Vai cuidar de quem realmente é maltratado”.

Os participantes afirmam que a transferência representa um risco para o animal e pode comprometer a saúde e o bem-estar dele. Entre os argumentos, os manifestantes citam a idade avançada de Sandro e os possíveis impactos de uma viagem longa. Eles também temem que a adaptação a um novo ambiente possa afetar o animal.

Sobre os protestos, o presidente do santuário afirmou que o local oferece aos elefantes uma oportunidade de ter uma vida com mais tranquilidade e conforto, algo que, segundo ele, muitos animais talvez nunca tivessem.

"A gente tá dando para esses animais uma vida que no zoológico nunca ia poder dar. Desde espaço, estrutura, atendimento especializado, pessoas capazes, até uma área muito maior. Para você ter ideia, a área que o Sandro vai ficar é maior do que o próprio zoológico inteiro de Sorocaba. É uma proporção que a gente não consegue nem comparar", ressalta o presidente.

🐘 Conheça as outras elefantas do Santuário

Atualmente moram no Santuário as elefantas Baby, Maia, Rana, Mara, Bambi e Guillermina. Conheça um pouco sobre cada uma:

Nascida em 1992, no estado da Flórida, nos Estados Unidos, Baby passou parte da vida em um circo antes de ser levada para o parque Beto Carrero World. — Foto: Santuário dos Elefantes Brasil

Nascida em 1992, no estado da Flórida, nos Estados Unidos, Baby passou parte da vida em um circo antes de ser levada para o parque Beto Carrero World, em Santa Catarina, onde se tornou uma das atrações.

A elefanta se tornou a segunda moradora mais jovem do Santuário, ficando atrás apenas de Guillermina, que possui 25 anos.

Maia, uma elefanta asiática de cerca de 50 anos, foi a primeira moradora do Santuário. — Foto: Santuário dos Elefantes Brasil

Maia, uma elefanta asiática de cerca de 50 anos, foi a primeira moradora do Santuário. Antes de chegar, em outubro de 2016, ela passou aproximadamente 30 anos em circos . Após ser retirada dessa situação, permaneceu por cinco anos acorrentada em uma fazenda , sem um local adequado para viver.

Conhecida pela personalidade dócil e pela energia intensa , Maia se tornou um dos símbolos do santuário. Segundo os cuidadores, ela superou os medos trazidos pelo passado em cativeiro e passou a demonstrar comportamentos mais naturais à medida que ganhou espaço para explorar.

Apaixonada por comida, especialmente mangas, a elefanta também é descrita como cooperativa e carinhosa, características que ajudaram em seu processo de adaptação e recuperação.

Rana, uma elefanta asiática de cerca de 65 anos, chegou ao Santuário em dezembro de 2018. — Foto: Santuário dos Elefantes Brasil

Rana, uma elefanta asiática de cerca de 65 anos, chegou ao Santuário em dezembro de 2018. Antes do resgate, ela viveu cerca de 40 anos em circos e passou os últimos anos em um zoológico no litoral brasileiro. Conhecida por sua capacidade de se adaptar aos outros elefantes, Rana é considerada pelos cuidadores uma espécie de "comitê de boas-vindas" do santuário.

Segundo a equipe do SEB, a elefanta passou por uma grande transformação após a chegada ao local. Inicialmente reservada e distante , ela se tornou uma das moradoras mais comunicativas do santuário , famosa pelas vocalizações que faz ao longo do dia. Rana também demonstrou evolução no convívio social com as demais elefantas e passou a explorar comportamentos naturais, como nadar, tomar banhos de lama e aproveitar os espaços abertos.

De acordo com os cuidadores, ela transmite sinais constantes de bem-estar e continua avançando em seu processo de recuperação após décadas em cativeiro.

Mara, uma elefanta asiática de cerca de 58 anos, chegou ao Santuário em maio de 2020. — Foto: Santuário dos Elefantes Brasil

Mara, uma elefanta asiática de cerca de 58 anos, chegou ao Santuário em maio de 2020. Nascida na Índia, ela foi levada ainda jovem para um zoológico na Alemanha e, posteriormente, para circos na América do Sul. Desde 1995, vivia no então Zoológico de Buenos Aires, na Argentina, onde permaneceu por mais de duas décadas até ser transferida para Mato Grosso.

Após uma vida marcada pelo confinamento, Mara chegou ao santuário com alguns problemas de saúde, incluindo lesões nas patas e no tornozelo dianteiro direito . Apesar de ter sido considerada agressiva em parte da vida, os cuidadores descrevem a elefanta como dócil, comunicativa e bastante afetuosa.

Conhecida pelas vocalizações frequentes, ela desenvolveu uma forte ligação com a elefanta Rana logo após chegar ao SEB. Segundo a equipe, Mara segue em processo de recuperação física e emocional, ganhando mais confiança e aproveitando a liberdade e os espaços amplos oferecidos pelo santuário.

Bambi, uma elefanta asiática de cerca de 60 anos, chegou ao Santuário em setembro de 2020. — Foto: Santuário dos Elefantes Brasil

Bambi, uma elefanta asiática de cerca de 60 anos, chegou ao Santuário em setembro de 2020. Antes do resgate, ela passou mais de 40 anos em circos e, após ser apreendida, viveu por cerca de uma década em zoológicos no interior de São Paulo . Quando foi transferida para Mato Grosso, apresentava baixo peso, pouca massa muscular e perda da visão de um dos olhos.

Apesar das condições de saúde encontradas no momento do resgate, Bambi surpreendeu os cuidadores ao demonstrar uma personalidade ativa e curiosa . Descrita como brincalhona e facilmente empolgada, ela passou a explorar os espaços do santuário com entusiasmo e a apresentar comportamentos mais naturais. Segundo a equipe do SEB, a elefanta ganhou autonomia, cuidados individualizados e melhores condições de bem-estar, fatores que contribuíram para sua recuperação física e emocional após décadas de cativeiro.

Guillermina, uma elefanta asiática de 25 anos, nasceu no Ecoparque de Mendoza, na Argentina, e passou toda a vida em cativeiro — Foto: Santuário dos Elefantes Brasil

Guillermina, uma elefanta asiática de 25 anos, nasceu no Ecoparque de Mendoza, na Argentina, e passou toda a vida em cativeiro antes de ser transferida para o Santuário. Filha das elefantas Pocha e Tamy, ela cresceu em um recinto com espaço extremamente limitado, onde tinha poucas oportunidades para explorar comportamentos naturais da espécie.

Descrita pelos cuidadores como curiosa, brincalhona e dona de uma personalidade marcante , Guillermina chegou ao santuário ainda muito dependente da mãe e insegura diante das novidades. Com a adaptação ao novo ambiente, passou a descobrir gradualmente elementos que nunca havia experimentado, como áreas amplas, vegetação, lama e o convívio com outros elefantes.

Segundo a equipe do SEB, a jovem elefanta segue desenvolvendo autonomia e habilidades sociais, enquanto explora o espaço e constrói novas relações após uma vida inteira em confinamento.

Para conhecer o Santuário não é preciso ir lá, até porque os elefantes vivem soltos e se escondem na mata, e a intenção é justamente que eles não sejam uma atração como foram durante a vida toda nos cativeiros onde viveram.

No entanto, nas redes sociais e no portal é possível acompanhar os relatos do dia a dia destes animais, assim como assistir aos vídeos que os tratadores conseguem fazer durante o atendimento a elas.

Quem quiser ajudar de forma mais efetiva, pode participar da campanha "Adotar um Elefante", enviando recursos especialmente para os cuidados de qualquer uma das moradoras.

articles.standfirst: Prazo termina às 17h para cursos em Gastronomia e Beleza; programa oferece 100 horas de aulas presenciais e módulos de empreendedorismo.
articles.summary: Prazo termina às 17h para cursos em Gastronomia e Beleza; programa oferece 100 horas de aulas presenciais e módulos de empreendedorismo.
articles.body:
Capacitações gratuitas preparam moradores para o mercado de trabalho e para a geração de renda — Foto: Arquivo Secom

Esta sexta-feira (18) é a última oportunidade para quem deseja garantir uma das 2,7 mil vagas gratuitas ofertadas no segundo ciclo do programa Qualifica + Macaé. As inscrições terminam às 17h, tanto na página oficial da Prefeitura quanto no atendimento presencial distribuído pelo município. A iniciativa é voltada prioritariamente para jovens, trabalhadores e pessoas que buscam inserção produtiva, primeiro emprego ou geração de renda.

Os cursos oferecidos nesta fase contemplam as áreas de Estética e Beleza (Cabeleireiro, Design de Sobrancelhas e Maquiagem Profissional) e Gastronomia e Alimentação (Panificação e Confeitaria). Cada capacitação possui carga horária de 100 horas, combinando formação básica, conteúdo técnico-prático e orientações focadas em empreendedorismo e mercado de trabalho. As aulas ocorrem nos turnos da manhã e da noite.

Atendimento presencial e polos de aula estão espalhados por dez bairros do município — Foto: Arquivo Secom

Para participar, o candidato deve ter no mínimo 16 anos completos no início do curso e preencher os requisitos do edital. O processo seletivo leva em consideração a ordem de chegada dos registros válidos. O edital também assegura inclusão e acolhimento, destinando 5% das vagas para pessoas com deficiência (PcD) e até 5% para mulheres em situação de violência doméstica — com atendimento presencial e sigiloso realizado via rede de assistência social.

A documentação exigida não precisa ser enviada na inscrição, sendo necessária apenas na etapa de confirmação de matrícula. Os convocados deverão apresentar documento com foto, CPF, comprovante de residência atualizado, comprovante de escolaridade (Ensino Fundamental incompleto) e, no caso de menores de 18 anos, autorização e documento do responsável legal.

A publicação do resultado final ocorre no dia 26 de setembro. Os aprovados deverão comparecer obrigatoriamente à aula inaugural no dia 29 de setembro, às 18h, no Centro de Convenções de Macaé, para garantir a vaga. articles.title: UK weather: Sunshine returns as warmer and drier weather arrives next week
articles.summary: High pressure over the UK next week will bring a break from the wet and windy weather so far this month.
articles.body:
Don't pack away your summer clothes just yet as warmer and drier weather could be set to return to the UK next week.

Temperatures could reach as high as 25C in parts of England and Wales - several degrees above the average for the time of year.

Forecasts for early next week show an area of high pressure building near the UK. This will largely block Atlantic weather systems, which often bring wind and rain, from reaching the country.

North-west Scotland will see some rain but these systems are not expected to push across the rest of the UK, so this would mean drier weather with lighter winds and higher daytime temperatures for most.

The last few weeks have been very changeable with rain and strong winds in most parts of the UK.

Despite this, the whole of Wales and most of England are still in drought.

After stronger south-westerly winds are due to blow cloud and outbreaks of rain across from the west on Friday, the weather will start to settle down over the weekend.

The northern half of the UK will see a return to sunshine and blustery showers on Saturday, with most of the showers being in Scotland.

The southern half of the UK is likely to be more cloudy and have a muggy feel with the chance of light rain and drizzle.

At least seven months of relentless rain needed to end drought, research shows

This rain will clear to the south on Sunday and most places will then be dry with sunny spells. West to north-west winds will still be strong in Scotland.

Temperatures will peak around 22C in southern England on Sunday - nothing out of the ordinary for the time of year.

But as we go into the working week, an area of high pressure will arrive, bringing drier weather, lighter winds, and some sunshine, which for much of the country could last throughout the week.

While there will still be the chance of catching the odd shower, most places will be dry. Rain-bearing bands of cloud coming in from the Atlantic will be restricted to north-west Scotland.

The past week has felt quite chilly but temperatures next week are forecast to reach 20C in Scotland and Northern Ireland, and as high as 25C in England and Wales.

This is some way off the UK's September temperature record, though, which stands at 35.6C, set in 1906 at Bawtry in South Yorkshire.

Autumn is often a time of wild swings in the weather.

This upcoming quieter spell in the UK is not influenced by the record-breaking Pacific Ocean warming from El Niño , but there could be impacts later in the autumn.

The Met Office long range forecast shows a higher degree of confidence that deeper areas of low pressure will affect the UK in November, potentially bringing stormy weather. This is consistent with weather patterns during El Niño events at this time of year.

But no two El Niños are the same - so, while it may increase the chance of certain types of weather occurring, this is not guaranteed.

Keep up to date with the forecast where you are on the BBC Weather website and app .

articles.title: US fans with Ed Sheeran tickets are 'torn' by Macklemore controversy
articles.summary: With Sheeran's next gig this weekend, some ticket holders said they were in two minds about going.
articles.body:
The snowballing controversy over pro-Palestinian rapper Macklemore being dropped as a support act for Ed Sheeran has plunged the tour into crisis and left concert-goers in the middle of the fraught Israel-Gaza debate.

Fans who spoke to the BBC - including those who have tickets to see Sheeran's next show - have been split since Macklemore was dropped from the Loop Tour this week after his "free Palestine" protest on stage.

All of Sheeran's opening acts have since quit in solidarity.

"I'm still torn," Damien Given told the BBC on whether he would attend Sheeran's show on Saturday, calling the artist's response disingenuous. Another fan called it a "no-win situation".

Since the controversy blew up earlier this week, ticket prices for his remaining shows in the US, Mexico and South America have dropped, as calls for boycotts spread.

Sheeran has responded , saying he's been "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine", but would not be drawn into a political debate.

He argued that "those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum" and stressed he was not responsible for Macklemore being removed from the tour.

Still, the backlash has come from all sides.

Some are upset Sheeran's tour is continuing without all the listed acts and they want refunds. It's no longer the show they paid for, they said.

Given, who is from Northern Ireland, said he's felt in two minds over the tickets he has on Saturday to see the show in Philadelphia.

It will mark Sheeran's first time back on stage since the controversy spiralled.

Given said he's felt that Macklemore was treated "very, very wrong" and thought Sheeran was not being transparent with fans.

"[Sheeran] said he was in support of Ukraine when the Ukraine-Russia war started," said Given.

"You can't just say now suddenly, 'I'm not political.'"

But he explained the poignant connection he's felt to Sheeran's music that has drawn him to Saturday's show.

The singer's hit Thinking Out Loud was the first dance at Given's wedding.

"When she danced," Given, 52, said, recalling the moment with his bride, "the first words of the song were, 'When your legs don't work like they used to before.'"

His wife, Kellie, had been diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and could barely walk. She died four years later, in 2024.

Given said if it wasn't for "that connection, I would absolutely" not be attending, but "I'm probably leaning towards going".

Fellow fan Patti Ann has felt less conflicted over the backlash and instead said Sheeran was in a "no-win situation".

"I back [Sheeran] 100% for his decision," she said. "I feel like he has an obligation and a contract with his venues, and sometimes, financially, you can't get out of those types of things."

Ann, who has been a Sheeran fan for years, said she thinks a concert venue is not the place for politics.

Believe what you want, she said, "just don't press it on me".

She still plans to attend his show in Atlanta, Georgia, in October.

Matt Jaye, a Jewish-American from Florida, said he was outraged watching Macklemore's comments on a New Jersey stage earlier this month in support of Palestine.

He contacted Ticketmaster and asked for a refund for tickets he has to Sheeran's November show in Tampa, Florida.

His request was denied, which he said was "pretty upsetting".

His mood changed, though, after Macklemore was removed from Sheeran's line-up.

"I'm not in favour of a one-sided presentation of things from an artist," Jaye, 48, said. "That's not why I'm going to the concert."

Jaye said he believed Sheeran bore some culpability for Macklemore's pro-Palestinian protest.

"If [Sheeran's] saying that he's apolitical, I would expect him to maintain those same standards for the artists that he's bringing on," he said.

"I don't think he handled it in the best way possible."

He added that he would have liked Sheeran to issue an apology to the Jewish community for making part of his audience "very uncomfortable".

Some fans are worried what will become of the tour by the time Sheeran is set to play in their city.

Heather Park, who has tickets this weekend, said she's worried some shows might be cancelled.

"My main thing was to go see Ed Sheeran," she said. "Macklemore was just a bonus."

While Park, 49, believes Macklemore's ouster was unfair and a violation of free speech, she said she's mostly unbothered by the drama and prefers to separate the artist from the art.

articles.title: 27 airframes of Tejas Mk1A jets ready, but 1-2 issues yet to be fixed; delivery of HTT-40 aircraft & Dhruv NG helicopter a milestone for all of us: HAL CMD Ravi K
articles.summary: News News: BENGALURU: Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) chairman and managing director Ravi K on Thursday said the aerospace organisation has already made read.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) chairman and managing director Ravi K on Thursday said the aerospace organisation has already made ready “27 airframes of advanced Tejas Mk1A (of the total 180), but there are one or two issues that are leading to delays in the delivery of the first batch of the advanced combat aircraft to the Indian Air Force”.Speaking to TOI in an interview at HAL’s biggest fighter jet complex in Bengaluru, Ravi K said, “We have received 10 engines from GE Aerospace. But there are one or two issues with the first batch of Tejas Mk1A which need further testing, like the integration of AESA (Active Electronically Scanned Array) radar. Maybe we are there at 90-95%, but the last 5% is still to be fixed. Another one (problem) is missile integration. A few tests are still pending. We need to fly Tejas with the missile (without firing it) to find out whether structurally everything is fine, like aerodynamically. I am not giving any exact timeline, but we are hopeful it (first batch of jets) will be done by this year.”On the more advanced version of the aircraft, Tejas Mk2, the HAL CMD said, “Tejas Mk 2 is an offshoot of Tejas Mk1A. Structure coupling is going on. It has come to that stage. We are planning to do the grounder (ground testing) by Feb. The F414 engine is a brand new engine. It is the first time the country is using it. Some tests will be required.”Denying that HAL is working on any Super Sukhoi programme, Ravi K said HAL is already “engaged in the design work for indigenising some systems of existing Su-30MK1 fighter jets like radar, though the project has not come to us”.On the licensed production of the 100-seat Russian SJ-100 regional passenger jet, the CMD said, “Currently we are trying to understand the technical aspect of the Russian aircraft SJ-100. What are the facilities required, what are the ecosystems required. All the technical discussions are continuing. Then we will enter the commercial aspect of it. We will sign the contract for transfer of technology. We have not put a timeline on it as it needs a lot of discussion.”The CMD said, “HAL is going into the Combat Air Teaming System (indigenous Indian manned-unmanned teaming programme). We are building the prototype.”Explaining the absence of HAL from the fifth-generation fighter jet AMCA programme, Ravi K said, “The entities participating in it had to partner with somebody. But HAL as a whole, it seems, was not meeting the parameters for the AMCA programme and therefore it has not been shortlisted for the programme.”On modernising HAL facilities, the CMD said, “We are spending on infrastructure across all the divisions. We will modernise all the divisions and all the hangars. We are investing in core activities, not non-core activities.”HAL is planning to establish maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) in foreign countries too. “We are looking for foreign partners that can establish MROs on their own in their country.”“I am very elated that we are going to deliver on Friday the remaining two Tejas trainer aircraft of the total 40 LCA Mk1 contract to the IAF. I had myself signed the contract. I am so happy that we are going to finish the delivery of the first contract. We are also going to deliver HTT-40 trainer aircraft to the IAF and finish the long-pending project. It is very critical for the IAF. You can’t sit on an LCA unless you have basic flight training. You have to first sit on a simulator and then HTT-40 and then NJT (New Jet Trainer). It is an important milestone for all of us as well as for the country. Besides them, we are going to hand over advanced Dhruv NG helicopters to Pawan Hans. The helicopter has multirole functions, like offshore (deployment) and medivac,” the CMD said, adding, a happy moment as “we will get the certification on Friday”.

articles.title: Houthis, Saudis, Iran - and the future of Middle Eastern oil
articles.summary: Middle East News: In a lightning offensive last week, Yemen’s Houthis took over much of the country’s Red Sea coast, threatening shipping in the vital sea lane that had.
articles.body: In a lightning offensive last week, Yemen’s Houthis took over much of the country’s Red Sea coast, threatening shipping in the vital sea lane that had emerged as an alternative to Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf. Houthis have been fighting a Saudi-led military coalition for a decade, although a 2022 UN-brokered truce halted their attacks on Saudi territory. But the Houthis’ latest move has once again sent oil prices north of the $100 per barrel mark, adding another front to the wider US-Israel war against Iran. Here’s the lowdown on why the Houthis’ Red Sea threat matters, how this puts Saudi Arabia in a serious pickle, and what it means for the Iran war:What’s the latest Houthi offensive all about?The offensive saw Houthis take over key parts of Yemen’s Red Sea coast. This adds weight to the Houthi threat to shipping in the vital sea lane. In fact, Houthis had earlier declared a blockade of Saudi ships in the region. Now they can seriously enforce this. Their mere presence along the coastline will make shippers jittery and raise insurance costs.Why is this a serious headache?With Strait of Hormuz effectively locked up by Iran and US, Red Sea had emerged as a vital alternative route, especially for energy trade out of the region. Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline was working at full capacity, transporting around 7 million barrels of oil daily across the breadth of the peninsula to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. This was a crucial lifeline for the global energy trade that had been severely restricted following the outbreak of the Iran war in Feb. But that East-West pipeline was hit by a drone attack last week — blamed on Iran-backed Shia militias in Iraq — to coincide with the Houthi advance on the Red Sea coast. Both operations seem to have been coordinated to put the choke on Red Sea shipping, which has to pass through the narrow Bab el-Mandeb strait that Houthis can now theoretically shut down.Why now?The timing of all this is not a coincidence. Actually, when the Iran war began, among Iran’s proxies in the region, Houthis held back. But in July, following the state funeral of Iran’s former supreme leader Ali Khamenei, an Iranian plane carrying the Houthi delegation back to Yemen was threatened by Saudi Arabia. Riyadh did not want that plane to land, and bombed the airport in the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital of Sanaa. But that plane landed anyway.Following the episode, Houthi rhetoric against the Saudis flared up. But the key development that may have pushed Houthis into action could be the American blockade of Iranian ports and shipping in Persian Gulf.By many estimates, that blockade appears to be working, and putting enormous pressure on the Iranian economy. Tehran is unable to push out its own oil, the Iranian rial has tanked, and Iranians have actually taken to saving eggs instead of hard cash. Plus, this is a strategy that plays into America’s strength — it can carry out a naval blockade for a far longer period than a continuous kinetic war against Iran.So, Iran, through the Houthi action, is sending the message that if oil can’t pass through Hormuz, any alternative routes, including through the Red Sea, will also be shut. In short, the energy trade in the region is handcuffed till the war is resolved.What do Houthis want? The Houthis’ main grievance is against the Saudis, whom they have been fighting since 2015. But, of course, as a member of Iran’s so-called ‘Axis of Resistance’, they are now being heavily supported by Tehran in terms of material and intelligence inputs. Especially since the Gaza and Iran wars have seen Tehran’s two main proxies in Hezbollah and Hamas take a huge battering. So, the Iranian Axis appears to be undergoing a recalibration, with Houthis and Iran-backed militias in Iraq taking a more leading role among the proxies. Ultimately Houthis want legitimacy. Their attacks against Saudi Arabia — they reportedly fired a drone at Mecca earlier this week — raise their profile. Their capture of the Red Sea coast gives them international attention. And these, in turn, see them emerge as the primary force in Yemen, instead of the internationally backed Yemeni transition govt. Obviously, all of this helps Iran.Why are Saudis in a jam?Because US has refused to directly intervene against Houthis this time. Washington is providing diplomatic and advisory support to Riyadh, but not much else. Saudis want missile and drone interceptors. But US stocks are running low, thanks to its war with Iran. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has similarly sought assistance from Egypt and UK. But no one is rushing military aid to Riyadh. Interestingly, even the recently inked Mecca Pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, and Pakistan hasn’t been activated.What are the takeaways?First, Houthis prove Iran’s Axis of Resistance is changing shape, with the Yemini militia taking a leading role. This has implications for both the Iran war, and security in Red Sea and Horn of Africa region. And second, alternative routes to Hormuz for energy transit, whether through sea or pipelines, are also not fully secure. They can be targeted by a host of Iran-backed militias in the region. This puts West Asia’s dominance in global energy supply under a serious cloud, perhaps forcing the international community to look for alternatives away from the region.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: While most Americans may hate datacenters, UAE minister calls them 'more important than roads'; and has a new ‘hiding rule’ for them after war destroyed many
articles.summary: Tech News News: The United Arab Emirates (UAE) will overhaul its regulatory framework for data centres and halt public disclosure of their physical locations to shiel.
articles.body: The United Arab Emirates (UAE) will overhaul its regulatory framework for data centres and halt public disclosure of their physical locations to shield them from military threats, according to comments reported by The Next Web of a session from Salesforce's annual event Dreamforce 2026. Speaking alongside Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff at the Dreamforce conference in San Francisco, Omar Sultan Al Olama, the UAE’s Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, Digital Economy and Remote Work Applications, warned that computing hubs have evolved into critical infrastructure that requires heightened protection.Al Olama said that data centres have become prime targets because our whole lives exist on connected devices, arguing that they are now more important than bridges, roads, or tunnels. In remarks highlighted in the 'The Next Web' report, the minister stated that the UAE will no longer promote the locations of these facilities to prevent bad actors from targeting them, adding that he expects other nations will soon be forced to adopt similar measures. "Unfortunately they’re more important than bridges. They’re more important than roads. They’re more important than tunnels because our whole lives are on these devices that we’re using," said Al Olama, in a session Salesforce published.Incidentally, UAE minister's views are very different from that of most Americans. While Donald Trump government strongly supports data centres, most states across the US are not in strong favour of them. The debate around data center projects is one of the rare modern issues to cut across party lines, demographics and geography -- uniting the US. As a report in AP says, from Republican-dominated Nebraska, Texas and Wyoming to swing-state Pennsylvania to Democratic-leaning New Mexico, in a divided America, the left and right unite to oppose AI data centers.How Iran war changed how UAE deals with data centers 'forever'The strategic shift comes in the wake of severe regional conflict that began on February 28, a day Al Olama recalled preparing for a trip to Ecuador before hostilities escalated. The UAE faced more than 1,000 projectiles and drones during the first week of the conflict alone, with launches from Iran taking only two minutes to reach the country. Al Olama noted that the UAE intercepted more aerial threats than the entire Middle East and Israel combined, resulting in zero impact on human lives or business operations. Domestic life has since returned to normal, though the government is now decentralizing key digital assets, including splitting up its domestic Stargate data centre project and investing in offshore facilities, such as in Germany.Reflecting on broader AI policy, Al Olama warned against allowing fear to choke innovation, drawing a historical parallel to the Middle East’s technological decline after centuries of dominance from 813 to 1515 AD. That era ended when the region banned the Gutenberg printing press for two centuries due to fears over misinformation, alterations to holy scripture, and general administrative anxiety. He cautioned that modern leaders cannot afford to repeat that mistake with artificial intelligence, even if the technology's rapid evolution initially seems frightening.When it comes to public deployment, Al Olama advocated a measured approach that avoids unproven, high-risk systems. UAE public services, such as Abu Dhabi’s TAMM administrative platform, run on established, older large language models rather than cutting-edge frontier systems like OpenAI’s Astra or Anthropic’s Fable, which he warned carry significant cybersecurity and data breach risks. He also drew hard red lines against using AI for predictive policing, citing the danger of false positives, and cautioned against building an oppressive surveillance apparatus, pointing instead to quality-of-life improvements like desk-free biometric airport transit.To insulate the domestic workforce from technological displacement, the UAE has trained all 80,000 federal civil servants in agentic AI, following an earlier initiative that taught prompt design to one million people. Al Olama dismissed fears of mass unemployment, insisting the technology will ultimately create opportunities and boost workforce capability.'One country regulating AI will not work, it has to be almost the entire world'Addressing the global regulatory landscape, Al Olama noted that governments typically overregulate while the private sector tends to underregulate. He pointed to the UAE’s own data protection laws, which were initially drafted by tech companies before state officials and civil society refined them, as a model for collaborative oversight. He warned Western policymakers that unilateral bans on AI would simply hand an insurmountable advantage to competitors, arguing that restrictions in the United States make little sense unless China agrees to follow suit.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: ‘Body kept in car for 7 hours’: How a Gurgaon meeting with ex-colleague ended in HR professional’s murder
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A 31-year-old HR professional, reported missing by his family after he went to Gurgaon to meet a former colleague, was allegedly murdered, .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A 31-year-old HR professional, reported missing by his family after he went to Gurgaon to meet a former colleague, was allegedly murdered, police have said.Delhi Police has arrested the former colleague, Anya Vats, and her partner Sanyam Sachdeva in connection with the alleged murder of Yuvraj Singh Manchanda. Police suspect a financial dispute to be behind the killing.Former colleague, partner arrestedAnya and Sanyam are both from Gurgaon. Police said the couple told investigators that they were married and had a one-year-old son. There are claims that Yuvraj was shot twice inside his own car, but police are verifying the details.Yuvraj lived with his family in Sarita Vihar. He used to work for a prominent real estate developer.“Anya had worked with Yuvraj in 2022 at another prominent real estate developer’s office and was currently unemployed. She was sacked from the company. We have learnt that some financial irregularities may have been the reason for her termination, but this is being verified,” police said.Sanyam too was unemployed, police added.Argument inside car before alleged killingSources said an argument happened inside Yuvraj’s car, after which he was allegedly murdered. The couple allegedly told police that they kept the body inside the car for at least seven hours while trying to figure out where to dump it.They later allegedly dumped the body in a sewer near their house. Then they fled to Uttarakhand.Yuvraj went to Gurgaon after meeting sistersYuvraj was missing from Sept 6 but the family lodged the complaint on Sept 11.On Sept 6, he went to a restaurant in Lajpat Nagar around 4pm. His family said he had gone shopping with his sisters before visiting the restaurant. He told the family he had a meeting in Gurgaon.Yuvraj then told his sisters to take a cab home and left for Gurgaon, sources said.According to the complaint, the family spoke to Yuvraj on the phone around 7pm, when he told them that he would be back home by 10pm. After that, his phone seemed to be switched off. The family could not reach him.His sister approached Lajpat Nagar police on Sept 11, following which a missing person FIR was registered.Call records, CCTV point to former colleagueInvestigators analysed call detail records, internet protocol data and CCTV footage and found out that Yuvraj had last spoken to Anya and had also told his family that he was going to Gurgaon to meet her.Both Yuvraj’s and Anya’s phones were switched off, prompting investigators to now track Anya’s movements. During the investigation, Anya emerged as a prime suspect.Investigators subsequently detected a new mobile number allegedly being used by Anya. Technical surveillance indicated she was in Uttarakhand. A police team was sent there and Anya and Sanyam were apprehended.Couple allegedly discloses murderPolice said the two disclosed their involvement in Yuvraj’s murder and told investigators that they had thrown his body into a drain near their house in Gurgaon.The disclosure led investigators to Badshahpur police station in Gurgaon, where an unidentified body was found in a drain on Sept 10. The body was badly decomposed.Police showed the photographs of the body to Yuvraj’s family, who identified him.Five-day police custodyAnya and Sanyam were arrested and produced in court, which sent them to five days’ police custody.Police are investigating the circumstances surrounding the killing, the alleged financial dispute, the exact roles of the accused and other aspects of the case, besides collecting forensic and technical evidence.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Trapped in traffic: Exam-bound kids take 2.5 hours to cover 4km in Bengaluru
articles.summary: BENGALURU: Hundreds of school-children commuting along the Varthur-Gunjur stretch of SH-35 endured a harrowing Thursday as severe traffic congestion d.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Hundreds of school-children commuting along the Varthur-Gunjur stretch of SH-35 endured a harrowing Thursday as severe traffic congestion delayed school buses by up to 40 minutes in the morning and left students stranded on roads for hours while returning home. A 4km drive took 2.5 hours, stuck mostly in traffic.The stretch hosts 18-20 big schools, with many conducting mid-term examinations. Parents told TOI children reached exam halls anxious after school buses arrived late at pickup points and were subsequently caught in gridlocked traffic.The evening commute was worse. Several students took up to 1.5 hours more to return home. Some schools accommodated affected students by providing extra time to complete exams.The Varthur-Gunjur stretch, part of SH-35, is undergoing infrastructure works being executed by Karnataka Road Development Corporation. However, residents say the corridor continues to be plagued by bottlenecks, damaged road surfaces, large craters and unmanaged traffic, making the daily commute unpredictable. Parents said Thursday’s situation highlighted how ongoing infrastructure issues were directly affecting schoolchildren.Priti Singh, a resident of Candor Landmark Apartments, said the biggest concern was that schools had exams. “It is unbelievable an area contributing significantly to the city’s economy continues to suffer from such poor infrastructure,” she added.Another resident, Pavitra Holla, said children were spending more time in traffic than in classrooms. “Today, some children took nearly 2.5 hours to cover just 4km from school. They are exhausted, parents are worried and there is no end in sight. There are no proper roads, heavy vehicles move during school hours, traffic management is absent and basic infrastructure is missing. Children are forced to sit in dust and traffic for hours,” she said. Holla added that while congestion has been a long-standing issue in the area, conditions have deteriorated in the past two weeks.For some parents, the situation left them with little choice but to abandon school buses and attempt the journey themselves.Swati Kumari, another resident of Candor Landmark, said she waited nearly 45 minutes for her son’s school bus before deciding to take him on a two-wheeler. “My son studies in a school less than 2km away from home. Though his school ends by 2.45pm, he’s been reaching home around 4.30pm in the past month. articles.title: Niger state: 37 suspected illegal miners die in Nigerian custody
articles.summary: Authorities linked the deaths to disease, but this has been disputed by intelligence reports and relatives of the accused.
articles.body:
Thirty-seven people accused of illegal mining in north-central Nigeria have died in custody, local officials said.

Police have set up an investigation into the deaths, which the Nigerian Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) blamed on an apparent disease outbreak.

However, an intelligence report shared with AFP news agency suggested the group died because of overcrowding and poor ventilation inside the detention facility in the Nigerian state of Niger.

State governor Mohammed Umaru Bago called the deaths "sad and tragic" during a press conference on Thursday.

An NSCDC commander has been detained following the deaths, Bago added.

He declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for elections scheduled for January.

Officials had arrested the group of young men on Tuesday for suspected illegal mining near Borgu, in the mineral-rich state of Niger. The region is known for small-scale gold mining.

Two days later, 37 people detained as part of the suspected unlawful operation were found dead inside the detention centre run by the NSCDC.

The NSCDC had earlier said the detainees were possibly victims of a diphtheria outbreak, a serious bacterial infection that can be fatal.

But the agency's national headquarters later said the cause had not been established and would require medical and laboratory tests.

"The NSCDC wishes to clarify that reports attributing the deaths to any specific disease remain subject to medical and laboratory confirmation," it added in a statement.

A survivor told the Associated Press news agency that about 65 people had been held in an overcrowded and poorly ventilated cell, suggesting the dead may have suffocated.

Some relatives of the deceased have disputed the official explanation of events, claiming to local media that they were deliberately killed.

One father told Nigerian media that his son had appeared healthy when relatives brought him food the day before his death and called for an independent post-mortem examination.

Another relative, whose 17-year-old brother was among those who died, said the family had visited him during his detention and questioned how a disease could have killed so many detainees without apparently affecting their guards.

Post-mortem examinations are expected to help establish what happened.

Niger's police chief ordered an immediate investigation into "the unfortunate death of suspected illegal miners while in the detention facility of the NSCDC", spokesman Wasiu Abiodun wrote in a statement.

The victim's bodies have since been taken to the general hospital in nearby Minna for examination.

The scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger state has been blamed for fuelling criminal gang violence, according to officials and experts.

Much of the gold in the region is trafficked through global supply chains, a 2024 SwissAid report found.

articles.title: Human-caused warming helped prime slope for deadly Nepal-Tibet flood, first study finds
articles.summary: South Asia News: Human-caused climate change likely helped destabilise rock-and-ice slope whose collapse triggered the Aug 26 Nepal-Tibet disaster, first scientific as.
articles.body: Human-caused climate change likely helped destabilise rock-and-ice slope whose collapse triggered the Aug 26 Nepal-Tibet disaster, first scientific assessment of the deadly event released Thursday found, linking decades of warming to thinning glaciers, thawing permafrost and more rain replacing snow.“There’s absolutely no doubt that human-induced climate change played a role here in the preconditioning of the disaster through permafrost thawing, through thinning of the glaciers, through having more rainfall instead of snow,” said Friederike Otto, climatologist at Imperial College London and co-author of World Weather Attribution (WWA) study.Researchers described it as a cascading disaster rather than conventional flood. Around 2 sq km of rock wall and glacier ice collapsed from Langtang Lirung at about 5,150 metres, plunging around 1,400 metres before turning into a debris flood. Water, rock, ice and sediment then travelled around 22km to Rasuwagadhi in seven minutes, leaving downstream settlements with almost no warning.The study found long-term warming had pushed freezing levels higher and exposed previously frozen rock and permafrost to prolonged thawing, weakening material binding steep slopes. July and Aug were exceptionally warm, with researchers estimating human-caused climate change added around 1.5C to temperatures, while heavy snowfall in late 2025 may have supplied additional meltwater. Nepal’s 2015 magnitude-7.8 earthquake could also have weakened mountain slopes, though researchers could not quantify its role.Priyanka Vadrevu, an independent researcher specialising in climate adaptation and disaster resilience, told TOI, “Rising temperatures are thinning ice, thawing permafrost and weakening frozen material that helps hold steep slopes together. Preparedness in the Himalayas can no longer focus only on rainfall and conventional flood forecasting. We need integrated monitoring of glaciers, permafrost, slopes, rivers and weather conditions.Nepal now hopes to seek around $20 million (£15 million) from UN Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, which supports countries facing climate-related destruction. The study is expected to strengthen Kathmandu’s case by linking warming to conditions that contributed to slope failure.The findings will also feed into Nepal’s diplomatic push next week. PM Balendra Shah will travel to New York from Sept 22-26 for UN General Assembly — his first foreign trip since taking office — where govt says he will highlight Aug 26 disaster, Nepal’s Himalayan vulnerability and demand greater climate justice and financing for countries bearing disproportionate losses from global warming.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: UK's 'dismal' Eurovision song choices to be examined by MPs
articles.summary: It comes after the UK's entry Look Mum No Computer came last in May's final, scoring just one point.
articles.body:
The UK's "dismal" record in selecting songs and acts for Eurovision is to be scrutinised by MPs.

In May, Look Mum No Computer came last with one point. In 2023 Mae Muller finished second from bottom and in 2021 James Newman came last - this time with "nul points".

The act that represents the UK is selected by the BBC, sometimes with a record label or music management company.

The chair of the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport committee, Dame Caroline Dinenage, said: "We want to get to the bottom of who chooses our entrant, on what basis and whether our dismal record of achievement in recent years [Sam Ryder to one side] is the result of bad song choice, weak performance... or something else".

It's expected that figures from the BBC, as well as music industry experts, will be called to give evidence to the committee of cross-party MPs at a hearing that will be held "over the coming months". The committee is also likely to receive relevant written submissions.

UK music success rarely repeated at Eurovision

Although the UK has, over the years, produced some of the world's most successful artists, that kind of success has rarely been repeated at Eurovision .

Over the past 15 years, the UK has only come higher than 15th place on one occasion - when Sam Ryder came second with his song Space Man in 2022. He was beaten by Ukraine's Kalush Orchestra.

And next year's event, being held in Burgas in Bulgaria, will mark 30 years since the UK last won the contest, when Katrina and the Waves scored 227 points with their song Love Shine A Light.

Many countries choose their entry through a publicly televised selection process.

The last time this was done in the UK was with the show Eurovision: You Decide in 2019. Michael Rice was selected, but went on to come last at the contest in Tel Aviv, Israel.

The MPs' hearing will be part of the committee's State of Play inquiry, where members of the public or others can request an evidence session to be held into a particular subject that interests or concerns them.

Dame Caroline told BBC News: "This application interested us because of the UK's reputation for scoring 'nul points', coming bottom, or close to bottom in recent years at Eurovision, despite having world-class song writers and musicians."

The Eurovision final has consistently been one of the UK's most popular music events, with millions staying up late to watch the final result.

No time frame for the select committee hearing has been set yet, but once all the evidence has been examined, it's expected that the committee may produce a short report containing recommendations to the BBC.

articles.title: 'Don't be silly' over Falklands and Irish unity, shadow foreign secretary tells Trump
articles.summary: Shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat says the US president's recent comments were aimed at US voters, in a BBC interview.
articles.body:
The shadow foreign secretary has told Donald Trump "don't be silly" over his comments on the UK's sovereignty of the Falkland Islands and Irish reunification.

Conservative MP Tom Tugendhat said the US president was trying to appeal to voters at home by making comments about the British overseas territory in the Atlantic Ocean and saying he would "love" to see a united Ireland.

Trump has said America's position on the Falklands is "one of many" under review, and hinted he would not help the UK in any potential future conflict with Argentina.

And the US president said on a visit to Ireland last week that Irish reunification was "going to happen eventually" and it would be a "great thing".

Britain and Argentina still dispute the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands, four decades on from an armed conflict there which the UK won.

Argentina's president heightened tensions with the UK over the Falkland Islands earlier this month, saying in a presidential address that "winds of change" favoured his country's claim to the islands.

He warned he will impose economic sanctions on firms which exploit oil nearby.

In response, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK's position on the islands was "unwavering", and they would remain British as "that is the overwhelming position of the Islanders."

And Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has hit back strongly over the issue, insisting "the Falkland Islands are British" and that Britain's continued connection with them "is of vital importance".

But Tugendhat, the Tory MP for Tonbridge in Kent who Badenoch appointed her shadow foreign secretary in a reshuffle earlier this month, has suggested Trump does not mean it.

"What he's doing is he's bumping his gums on some issues that he thinks are supportive to various electoral issues for himself at home," he told Nick Robinson on Political Thinking.

"He's got elections coming up in November, he knows he's got votes to win.

"Is it helpful to us? No. But this is his politics, not ours. So sometimes we have to say something and sometimes we have to go, 'come on mate, don't be silly'."

Tugendhat explained that Britain's military capability in the Falklands is radically different from in 1982, when the UK and Argentina fought for 74 days over the territory, with the UK Foreign Office not negotiating to give the islands up in recent years.

And asked about Trump saying he would "love to see" Irish reunification on a recent trip there, Tugendhat branded this "plain old electioneering," ahead of US mid-term elections in November.

"Is he going to do anything about it? No," he added.

Elsewhere in his interview, Tugendhat revealed he had received no confirmation from China that the country's sanctions against him had been dropped.

This is despite then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer announcing they had been in January.

He said he would only visit China, whose communist regime he has long criticised, if there was something relevant and worth discussing - but he feels talks can be held elsewhere at the moment.

He also said Miliband should have waited rather than showing "weakness" after the UK sanctioned illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

And he ruled out bringing Britain back into the European Union if in government, despite his close personal ties to the continent including his French wife who was influential in the recent Bayeux Tapestry exchange.

Having run against Badenoch for Tory leader in 2022, he praised her performance as leader so far - saying her hoping to be Britain's next prime minister was a weight off his own shoulders.

articles.title: Singer Harry Styles funds free coffee at two London cafes
articles.summary: The singer funded free coffees for customers at Kaffeine's two central London cafes on Saturday.
articles.body:
Harry Styles bought coffees for all of the visitors to his "favourite" London coffee shop to celebrate the extension of his record-breaking Together, Together tour.

The singer funded free coffees for all of the customers at Kaffeine's two central London cafes on Saturday through promoter Live Nation.

Owner Peter Dore-Smith said he was not allowed to promote the free drinks on social media, but could tell customers that they had been bought by Together, Together, the name of the artist's tour.

Dore-Smith said he was told by Live Nation that his company was chosen as Styles' "favourite coffee shop", but the free drinks could not be promoted beforehand.

The owner said Styles covered the usual Saturday takings at both sites on Eastcastle Street and Great Titchfield Street and also added a buffer to ensure all drinks could be paid for.

Dore-Smith said that the star had visited his Eastcastle Street coffee shop "a couple of years ago", and that they put his song lyrics on their blackboard during his last concerts in London.

On the day of the giveaway, Dore-Smith said they placed posters in the window and put Together, Together tour stickers provided by the promoter on every cup of coffee they sold.

Styles' music played in the shops and staff wore ties to "dress up" like the artist, who often performs wearing the accessory.

"We put extra staff on, and on the day people just rocked up as normal," Dore-Smith said.

When customers asked why their drink was free, his staff told them "because Harry Styles is buying everyone's coffee today," he said.

He added: "I know they've done it with a florist before, and I think they've done it with an ice cream parlour before."

articles.title: Odyssey painting goes on show at York Art Gallery
articles.summary: The work by Turner is on loan from the National Gallery and forms part of a new exhibition in York.
articles.body:
A famous painting depicting a scene from Homer's Odyssey has gone on display at York Art Gallery.

The J.M.W. Turner creation, on loan from the National Gallery and forming part of a new exhibition, shows Ulysses, also known as Odysseus, sailing from the island where Polyphemus, a one-eyed giant, had held him and his men captive.

Following the recent success of the new Christopher Nolan film based on the epic poem, curators said they hoped there would be renewed interest in artists' interpretations of Homer's work.

The painting is one of more than 100 works to go on display as part of Turner, Wedgwood & Beyond: Inspired by Flaxman, which opens at the gallery on Friday.

The exhibition looks at work by John Flaxman, a York-born artist, on the 200th anniversary of his death, as well as the artists he inspired.

Senior curator Dr Beatrice Bertram said: "Flaxman may not be a household name these days, but what we hope to do within this show is to really redress him and give him some time in the light again.

"In his time, he was internationally renowned for his sculptures and his designs, particularly his illustrations of Homer's Iliad and Odyssey."

According to the show's curators, elements of Flaxman's sketches can be seen in Turner's painting called Ulysses Deriding Polyphemus – Homer's Odyssey, including outlines of horses in the sunset and the shadow of a cyclops.

The works are shown side by side on the gallery wall, inviting visitors to compare them.

Co-curator Richard Johns, from the University of York, said the exhibition had not been planned around the release of the film, but was rather a "happy accident".

"It wasn't actually something we had in mind when we were developing the exhibition, or even when we asked the National Gallery if they would lend this painting," he explained.

"The interest in the Odyssey as a poem has increased enormously as a result of the success of the film.

"I hope it will encourage people who've seen the film or have a renewed interest in Homer to come and see what artists in the 18th and 19th Century made of Homer's poetry, just as we've seen how an artist like Christopher Nolan in the 21st Century interprets those same ideas."

The exhibition will be on display until 17 January 2027.

articles.title: F-35 sale to Saudi Arabia cleared after years of to and fro between Washington and Riyadh
articles.summary: International News: After years of hesitation, Washington has finally moved to sell Saudi Arabia the F-35, its most advanced stealth fighter, ending a saga that has dragg.
articles.body: After years of hesitation, Washington has finally moved to sell Saudi Arabia the F-35, its most advanced stealth fighter, ending a saga that has dragged on for years amid concerns over transferring the aircraft to a West Asian power may dilute Israel's aerial dominance vis-a-vis its neighbours. The US State Department cleared the potential Foreign Military Sale of up to 48 F-35A Lightning II jets to Riyadh, in a deal valued at USD 24.3 billion, notified to Congress on Thursday.The package goes well beyond the aircraft itself. It includes 49 Pratt & Whitney F135-PW-100 engines, one per aircraft plus a spare, alongside secure communications and navigation systems, cryptographic equipment, electronic warfare support, spare parts, simulators, training and extensive logistics support. The State Department said the sale would strengthen the defences of a major non-NATO ally and improve interoperability with US, regional and NATO forces, while explicitly stating it would not alter the existing military balance in the region, a clear nod to longstanding Israeli objections, since Israel remains the only Middle Eastern nation currently operating the F-35.The deal was cleared just days after Yemen's Houthi movement claimed to have shot down a Royal Saudi Air Force F-15 over Marib governorate on September 16. Video released by the group showed wreckage bearing a Saudi flag insignia, and if confirmed, this would mark only the second time a US-built F-15 has been downed by hostile fire, and possibly the fifth Strike Eagle lost in the region this year alone. Riyadh has not officially confirmed the loss.That vulnerability underlines exactly why Saudi Arabia has pushed so hard for the F-35. Unlike the ageing F-15 fleet, heavily exposed to increasingly sophisticated Houthi air defences cobbled together from repurposed air-to-air missiles and Iranian-derived systems, the F-35's stealth characteristics are designed to evade precisely this kind of threat environment.The approval also follows a string of other major Saudi arms purchases this year, including a 5 billion dollar bomb deal, a 750 million dollar tank engine package, and a USD 1.96 billion precision-guidance kit agreement, signalling Riyadh's broader rearmament push amid an increasingly volatile regional security picture.While the sale still requires congressional approval and no contract has yet been signed, its approval marks a genuine shift in longstanding US policy, one that had kept its most advanced stealth fighter out of Gulf Arab hands for years, until mounting battlefield losses appear to have tipped the calculus toward finally saying yes.The UAE was also seeking to procure the F-35 and this effort went back to 2020 deal. This deal was signed alongside the Abraham Accords, when Washington agreed to sell Abu Dhabi up to 50 F-35s as part of a broader USD 23 billion package that also included armed drones and other advanced munitions. The agreement was seen as a reward for the UAE's normalisation of ties with Israel. Negotiations stalled repeatedly, and the deal was formally suspended in late 2021 after the UAE itself paused talks over what it called unacceptable conditions and sovereignty restrictions attached to the sale. With the F-35 deal in limbo, the UAE pivoted instead to France, signing a landmark deal for 80 Rafale fighters in December 2021, a purchase worth around 19 billion dollars, its largest-ever defence acquisition.

articles.title: Royal Exchange: Costume exhibition celebrates 50 years of city's 'spaceship-like' theatre
articles.summary: To mark the anniversary of the seven-sided theatre constructed from tubular steel, some archive costumes go on display.
articles.body:
Fifty years ago, the Royal Exchange Theatre in Manchester opened its doors for its first production of Richard Brinsley Sheridan's The Rivals.

It was September 1976, and the seven-sided theatre constructed from tubular steel in the heart of the city was described by some as something from out of space.

"It sits almost like a spaceship inside this extraordinary great Victorian Hall with all the pillars so already you have this tension," said Selina Cartmell, the theatre's creative director.

"They created a theatre of 750 seats in the round, a democratic arena where the alchemy between actor and audience is at its most purest form and they've created something that still feels fresh today."

In the five decades since the theatre opened in St Ann's Square, some of the world's most famous actors have performed at the theatre.

Hugh Grant in 1986 and Bob Hoskins and Helen Mirren in 1981 are just some of the acting talent to have graced its stage.

In 2004, long before Spiderman, Andrew Garfield was in Cares, while Maxime Peake appeared more recently in 2015 and the following year Don Warrington swapped Death in Paradise to play King Lear.

To mark its 50th anniversary, some of the costumes worn by those acting greats are on display.

The Mythic Reinvention exhibition, which is free, includes just a small fraction of the theatre's collection.

There are more than 25,000 costumes and other items kept in its archive and all the outfits for its performances are made in-house.

It aims to provide an exclusive insight into the inner workings of the theatre's costume department from the artists who created some of the Royal Exchange's most iconic shows.

The exhibition has been curated by award-winning designer Leslie Travers.

"To think there are so many pieces of costume here from so many productions," he said.

"I think Manchester should be incredibly proud of this building because the costume-making is world famous.

"It's amazing that these costumes, some of them are 50 years old but they look brand new. They've been so well looked after."

He added: "It's a big auditorium but it's incredibly intimate so the material selection has to be really considered because you get to look at the costumes close up."

Cartmell said the exhibition would "give audiences a never-seen-before look into what makes the Royal Exchange such a special place".

"It will be a chance to celebrate every individual who has helped create and shape this beloved theatre as we look to our future."

Mythic Reinvention: An exhibition celebrating 50 Years of Costume and Craft is open until 15 November.

articles.title: Give our southern villages tourism boost, say Rushen families
articles.summary: Visitor numbers and fears for the future for young people are clear topics ahead of the election.
articles.body:
Residents in the south of the Isle of Man have called for a fresh boost for tourism ahead of the island's forthcoming election, as well as highlighting pressures on local shops and concerns about young people.

The island's southern-most constituency, Rushen, takes in the villages of Port Erin and Port St Mary along with its namesake parish.

Traditionally dominated by fishing and farming, the seaside villages went on to benefit from the so-called "bucket and spade brigade" tourist boom - which later fell into decline.

That loss, along with the rising cost of living, is something of much concern to traders, including Port Erin gift shop owner Dawn Sim, who said people were "just not coming out".

She said: "This year's been the hardest, it's the world situation, the cost of energy, even if people have got money they're hanging on to it. It's just very, very difficult."

Her husband Rob Sim said although there had been a "shop local" drive by the government during the Covid pandemic, that message had since fallen away.

And government schemes to support businesses, although "well intentioned", had largely been focused on hospitality and retail "doesn't seem to come into any of their equations", he said.

"We are grateful to our locals who keep us going, but figures are down generally," he said. "I'm not just talking the income, but the number of people."

Dawn Sim added that changes to the TT schedule in recent years to introduce back-to-back race days meant the less footfall in the south from visitors.

Dan Blythe, who owns an antiques and vintage shop in Port Erin, said his business did not "particularly rely on tourism" which made him different the majority of shop holders in the village.

However, he said rates charged on commercial properties could be looked at as it was "something that affects all bricks and mortar businesses".

He said concessions for firms that need to use the government-owned ferry services "to make life easier for small business holders to do trade on and off the island" was also something that would help.

"If people don't want town centres to keep shrinking then let's make it easier for them."

Vivienne Clarke, who works part-time in the village's pet shop, agreed that everybody "works hard to keep these small shops going, and it becomes harder every year".

She said getting parking nearby could be an issue and 'disc zone' areas meant the time people could spend in the shops and cafes was limited.

"I think keeping the communities alive is the most important thing and affordable," she added.

Chris Beards, who runs a card shop in the high street in Port Erin, said improving the economy to make it possible for firms to grow was vital.

"If people have got money to spend then hopefully they spend it locally, and I think people want to support the local shops generally," he said.

Attracting more high-end cruise ships to the island "could be a really important market for us" in the south of the island, he explained.

"I think there's been a bit of a focus on tourism numbers rather than the quality of the person coming.

"If we could get sort of a more high-quality tourist over then it has to benefit the economy really, I can't see that it wouldn't."

"Definitely more people could be pushed to come down south," he said, by taking some of the focus off Douglas.

But Kay O'Meara, who runs a pub in neighbouring village Port St Mary, said attracting walkers was more beneficial to the hospitality trade as "they will come in for a pint".

Her son, Callum O'Meara, said although cruise passengers would sometimes come in, "usually you just wave as the coach goes by".

"We're better off bringing in hikers, because they will spend more money - they need places to stay, they have to buy things to eat."

Looking at the broader issues facing the constituency, Kay O'Meara said she saw "no future" for the younger generation in the village.

"I see we have young people that don't want to be here... there's nothing in place for them, there's no housing," she said.

"I feel disillusioned. I mean, I've had my life, I was born here, I love it, I don't want to live anywhere else, but I can't see much of a future for the likes of my son and his baby."

Other concerns raised within Rushen included access to GP appointments, foot path maintenance, mental health support, the state of High Street in Port St Mary, and the impact of the island's ageing demographics on the welfare bill.
