articles.title: Campaigners feel 'powerless' over future of East Pye solar farm
articles.summary: Developer Island Green Power says the project will generate enough power for 115,000 homes.
articles.body:
Campaigners speaking at a series of open floor hearings on the future of a 2,700-acre (about 1,000-hectare) solar farm say they feel powerless and dismissed.

Six months of hearings began on Tuesday on the future of the East Pye solar farm which, if approved, would be built on land near Long Stratton in Norfolk and would generate enough power for 115,000 homes.

Developer Island Green Power (IGP), said the solar farm would help the UK reduce its carbon emission and meet net zero targets.

But Sandra Mullet, who lives in Great Moulton, said: "There is a genuine sense of grief and fear in our communities. You have made us feel powerless, but we are not - and we should not - be dismissed as such."

The Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS) said that more than 60 people spoke during two open floor hearings on Tuesday and Wednesday at Dunston Hall in Norwich.

The project will stretch across a number of villages including Hempnall, Great Moulton and Saxlingham Nethergate.

The Conservative leader of South Norfolk Council, Daniel Elmer, said the district had already accommodated several major infrastructure projects, including renewable energy schemes.

He said: "The scale of this infrastructure is substantial and has already transformed parts of our rural landscape.

"This is not a debate about whether renewable energy is necessary. It is, but this particular scheme would not work for South Norfolk."

In documents submitted to the government, developer IGP estimated the project would cost £1bn to build including land acquisition, construction and installation costs.

Due to its size, the solar farm is considered nationally significant and is one of three major solar farms planned for Norfolk.

During the hearing on Wednesday, Kathy Thompson, from Great Moulton, told the Planning Inspectorate that the project "threatens everyone in Norfolk".

She said: "The reality is that many still have no idea of the terrifying scale of what is happening."

Opponents have also likened the project to HS2, the high-speed railway which will connect London and Birmingham.

Karl Catchpole, Reform UK councillor for Long Stratton, said: "We can't let East Pye solar become this region's HS2: a decision made far away, imposed on a community that is never totally listened to.

"South Norfolk has already contributed to this country's energy targets."

Previously, a spokesman for IGP said "solar energy is among the cheapest power produced in Great Britain, supporting the aim of reducing bills for homes and businesses".

The examination process is expected to conclude in February when inspector David Cliff will have three months to submit a recommendation to Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, who will have a further three months to make a decision.

articles.title: Perth shark attack: swimmer missing after incident off Sorrento Beach in Western Australia
articles.summary: Emergency crews rushed to Sorrento Beach in Perth on Friday morning with a police search underway.
articles.body:
Police are searching for a swimmer missing in waters off the west coast of Australia after a suspected shark attack.

Emergency crews were called to a "shark-related incident" at Sorrento Beach in Perth, Western Australia around 10.15 local time on Friday.

Three St John ambulance crews attended, with local authorities confirming that "water police and the police air wing" remained at the scene as they searched for a missing person.

One witness described seeing a man being pulled under the water by a shark, just 50 metres off the shore, while another said they saw a "pool of blood" in the water, according to local media.

One witness told local outlet WAtoday that she saw the man being "mauled" as the shark "tossed him around like a fish".

"I'm a nurse, so I mean I obviously see a lot of gruesome stuff, but to see somebody being mauled to death in the water in front of me is pretty hard to clock," she told WAtoday.

"I only live just down the road, and I swim every day. I mean, there's no way I'm going to be getting in that water again."

Another witness said she was walking along the beach with a friend when the attack happened.

"I looked out to the ocean and I could see a pool of blood," Jacqui Rapaic told national broadcaster ABC.

The beach remains closed to the public and authorities have asked the public to avoid the area.

articles.title: Westhall community pub considers building its own wind turbine
articles.summary: Villagers are exploring ways to produce their own electricity in a bid to reduce costs.
articles.body:
Villagers who bought a pub and transformed it into a thriving local hub are exploring ways of generating their own electricity – including installing their own wind turbine.

Residents in Westhall, near Halesworth, Suffolk, became some of the first in England to secure funding to buy their own pub after winning a £96,000 government grant in 2021.

The local community had been running The Racehorse for two years before officially taking it over, after coming together to rent it following a more than three-year closure.

The campaigners who fought to keep the pub alive are now looking to go one further by building a community solar farm or wind turbine to reduce electricity costs.

Kim Hoare, one of the residents who spearheaded the pub takeover, said it provided the area with an opportunity to obtain further ownership of its services.

"Westhall is a fantastic village - it's already got its own community pub and it feels like it could really get to grips with its own community energy project," she said.

"We all know green energy is the direction of travel, and it's so much better to have ownership and control of it rather than have it imposed on you."

The plan is part of an initiative by the Halesworth Area Sustainability Hub, which strives to reduce the carbon footprint of communities and achieve self-sufficiency.

In addition to reducing electricity bills, it is hoped the project could make the village more accessible and less isolated.

Due to having no access to mains gas, more than half of households are currently reliant on oil or LPG to heat their homes.

Prescription medicines, meanwhile, have to be delivered to the pub for collection because the nearest pharmacy is four and a half miles away.

Buses from Westhall to Halesworth also only run once a day and residents without cars find it difficult to access basic services.

"Maybe an EV car you could borrow, or EV charging points, who knows? There are a whole range of possibilities for the community to explore," added Hoare.

The proposal will be discussed by villagers, parish councillors and landowners at a workshop meeting on 26 September before a study determines if it is feasible.

If doable, members of the community may be asked to help raise money in order to fund the project alongside a government grant - in the same way the pub was bought.

On Thursday, Downing Street's Great British Energy released £30m of a £1bn windfall of funding to support more than 1,000 community-led clean energy projects across the UK.

In Westhall, that could come in the form of a wind turbine, despite the previous construction of five turbines proving controversial.

"What would be more exciting would be an energy project owned by the community itself which could be wind turbines or solar panels," added Hoare.

"They'd get a discount and a say over what the people of Westhall wanted, where they wanted it and what benefits they would like to see from it."

articles.title: Family of Jagtar Singh Johal say detained Scot has been granted bail
articles.summary: Th Sikh activist from Dumbarton was arrested in 2017 in India in connection with alleged terror offences.
articles.body:
The family of a Scottish Sikh activist who has been locked up in India for almost nine years without conviction have said he has been granted bail.

Jagtar Singh Johal, from Dumbarton, was arrested in 2017 in connection with alleged terror offences.

He was arrested for his alleged role in a series of targeted killings of religious and political figures.

His family said they were still waiting for the details of what will happen next but are "relieved" by the Indian court's decision.

The 39-year-old was acquitted last year in a case in which he was accused of financially supporting a terror group, but he still faces federal charges by the Indian authorities.

Johal's imprisonment was recognised by a UN panel as arbitrary detention in 2022 and he has claimed to have been tortured.

Indian authorities have previously denied the torture claim and have repeatedly maintained due process is being followed.

He was arrested in the Punjab region just weeks after his wedding in the country.
